Let $k\ge1$, $d\ge1$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$, using the convention of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **constant-step $k$-step linear multistep method** has real coefficients $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_k,\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_k$ with $\alpha_k\ne0$ and advances values by

$$\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jY_{n+j}=h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j f(t_{n+j},Y_{n+j}),\qquad t_{n+j}=t_n+jh,\quad h>0.$$

Multiplying all coefficients by the same nonzero scalar leaves the method unchanged; one may normalize $\alpha_k=1$. Its **characteristic polynomials** are

$$\rho(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_j\zeta^j,\qquad \sigma(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j\zeta^j.$$

For an exact solution $y$ with $p+1$ continuous derivatives, the **unscaled local residual** at $t_n$ is

$$\tau_n(h;y)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jy(t_n+jh)-h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_jy'(t_n+jh).$$

The method has **order at least $p$**, where $p\ge1$ is an integer, if this residual is $O(h^{p+1})$ uniformly for admitted starting times in every fixed compact interval on which the indicated derivatives are bounded. It is **consistent** if it has order at least one. Equivalently, with the above coefficient convention, consistency is $\rho(1)=0$ and $\rho'(1)=\sigma(1)$.

The **root condition** is that every complex root of $\rho$ has modulus at most one and every root of modulus one has algebraic multiplicity one. The method is **zero-stable** if for each $T>0$ there is a constant $M_T$ independent of $N$ such that every solution of the homogeneous recurrence $\sum_j\alpha_jY_{n+j}=0$ on the uniform grid $h=T/N$ satisfies

$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|Y_n\|_\infty\le M_T\max_{0\le j<k}\|Y_j\|_\infty.$$

Here $\|x\|_\infty=\max_{1\le i\le d}|x_i|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The root-condition equivalence for zero-stability is established separately.

Let $K$ be a field, let $d\ge1$, and let $C$ be the row-shift companion matrix associated with

$$\chi(t)=t^d+c_1t^{d-1}+\cdots+c_d.$$

Then the matrix characteristic polynomial is exactly

$$\chi_C(t)=\det(tI_d-C)=t^d+c_1t^{d-1}+\cdots+c_d.$$

Let $a$ satisfy an order-$d$ recurrence from zero over a field, let $C$ be its row-shift companion matrix, and put $v_n=(a_n,\ldots,a_{n+d-1})^{\mathsf T}$. Then

$$v_{n+1}=Cv_n\qquad\text{and}\qquad v_n=C^nv_0$$

for every $n\ge0$.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[lem-complex-polynomial-growth-and-minimum-modulus]], [[lem-dalembert-minimum-modulus-descent]].

A field $F$ is **algebraically closed** when every nonconstant polynomial $p\in F[x]$ has a root in $F$: there is $\lambda\in F$ such that $p(\lambda)=0$.

This definition concerns roots in the field itself. It does not assert here that any particular field, including $\mathbb C$, is algebraically closed.
Every endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field has a Jordan canonical form over that field, including the endomorphism of the zero space.

A **Jordan basis over $F$** for an endomorphism $T:V\to V$ is an ordered basis obtained by concatenating Jordan strings for $T$, all with eigenvalues in $F$ ([[def-jordan-block-and-jordan-string]]). The matrix of $T$ in such a basis is block diagonal with blocks $J_m(\lambda)$ and is called a **Jordan canonical form of $T$ over $F$**.

The adjective “canonical” records the block multiset, not a prescribed order of blocks: permuting the strings usually changes the literal block diagonal matrix. On the zero space the empty basis and empty block matrix form the Jordan basis and Jordan form.

For $m\ge1$ and $\lambda\in F$, the **Jordan block** $J_m(\lambda)$ is the $m\times m$ matrix with $\lambda$ on the diagonal, $1$ on the superdiagonal, and $0$ elsewhere.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. A **Jordan string of length $m$ for $T$ at $\lambda$** is an ordered list $(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$ satisfying
$$(T-\lambda I)v_1=0,\qquad (T-\lambda I)v_j=v_{j-1}\quad(2\le j\le m).$$
Its **initial vector** is $v_1$ and its **terminal vector** is $v_m$. The initial vector is required to be nonzero; consequently every vector in the string is nonzero. In the ordered basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$, the restriction of $T$ to the string's span has matrix $J_m(\lambda)$ under the coordinate-column convention ([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]).

A Jordan string for a nilpotent endomorphism means a string at $\lambda=0$.

Let $A\in M_r(F)$ and $D\in M_s(F)$. For either block-triangular matrix

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&D\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{or}\quad M=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\C&D\end{pmatrix},$$

one has $\chi_M(x)=\chi_A(x)\chi_D(x)$, including $r=0$ or $s=0$.

derivations.claim: The companion matrix has characteristic polynomial $\rho/\alpha_k$ by [F2]. By [F4] and [F5], write $C=SJS^{-1}$ over $\mathbb C$, where $J$ is a block diagonal sum of Jordan blocks. Each block $J_m(\lambda)$ contributes $(z-\lambda)^m$ to the characteristic polynomial by [F6] and [F7]. Thus the algebraic multiplicity of each root of $\rho$ is the sum of the sizes of its Jordan blocks.

If $\rho$ has a root $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|>1$, the complex sequence $u_n=\lambda^n$ solves the homogeneous recurrence. If $\lambda$ is real, this is an unbounded real solution. If $\lambda$ is nonreal, its real and imaginary parts solve the real recurrence because the coefficients are real, and $\max(|\operatorname{Re}u_n|,|\operatorname{Im}u_n|)\ge |u_n|/\sqrt2$ for every $n$; hence at least one of those real solutions is unbounded along a subsequence. By [F3], the corresponding real solution has an initial state whose companion iterates are unbounded.

If a root $\lambda$ of modulus one has multiplicity $m\ge2$, write $\rho(z)=(z-\lambda)^m q(z)$. For the forward shift $E u_n=u_{n+1}$, $(E-\lambda)(n^s\lambda^n)=\lambda^{n+1}((n+1)^s-n^s)$, whose polynomial factor has degree $s-1$. Iterating $m$ times gives $(E-\lambda)^mu=0$ for $u_n=n^{m-1}\lambda^n$; since $q(E)$ commutes with $(E-\lambda)^m$, this sequence satisfies $\rho(E)u=0$, yet $|u_n|=n^{m-1}$ is unbounded. If coefficients are real and $\lambda$ is nonreal, the real and imaginary parts are real recurrence solutions and at least one is unbounded along a subsequence.
Suppose the root condition holds. If $|\lambda|=1$, its algebraic multiplicity is one by [F1], so its only Jordan block has size one.

For a block with $0<|\lambda|<1$, the binomial identity gives $J_m(\lambda)^n=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\binom nj\lambda^{n-j}N^j$. For each fixed $j$, the ratio of successive terms $n^j|\lambda|^{n-j}$ tends to $|\lambda|<1$, so this scalar sequence is bounded; if $\lambda=0$, the block powers vanish for $n\ge m$. A unit-modulus block has size one by step 2.1 and therefore has powers of modulus one. Finitely many blocks give $\sup_n\|J^n\|_\infty<\infty$.

For any matrices $A,B$, expanding entries and applying the triangle inequality gives $\|AB\|_\infty\le\|A\|_\infty\|B\|_\infty$. Hence $\|C^n\|_\infty\le\|S\|_\infty\|J^n\|_\infty\|S^{-1}\|_\infty$, uniformly in $n$.

Under the root condition, steps 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1 bound the powers of $C$. If it fails, steps 1.2–1.3 give an unbounded homogeneous mode, and [F3] turns that mode into an initial state with unbounded companion iterates. Thus the powers are bounded exactly under the root condition, and [F1] gives the equivalent zero-stability statement.

A **constant-step $k$-step linear multistep method** has real coefficients $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_k,\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_k$ with $\alpha_k\ne0$ and advances values by

$$\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jY_{n+j}=h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j f(t_{n+j},Y_{n+j}),\qquad t_{n+j}=t_n+jh,\quad h>0.$$

Multiplying all coefficients by the same nonzero scalar leaves the method unchanged; one may normalize $\alpha_k=1$. Its **characteristic polynomials** are

$$\rho(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_j\zeta^j,\qquad \sigma(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j\zeta^j.$$

For an exact solution $y$ with $p+1$ continuous derivatives, the **unscaled local residual** at $t_n$ is

$$\tau_n(h;y)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jy(t_n+jh)-h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_jy'(t_n+jh).$$

The method has **order at least $p$**, where $p\ge1$ is an integer, if this residual is $O(h^{p+1})$ uniformly for admitted starting times in every fixed compact interval on which the indicated derivatives are bounded. It is **consistent** if it has order at least one. Equivalently, with the above coefficient convention, consistency is $\rho(1)=0$ and $\rho'(1)=\sigma(1)$.

The **root condition** is that every complex root of $\rho$ has modulus at most one and every root of modulus one has algebraic multiplicity one. The method is **zero-stable** if for each $T>0$ there is a constant $M_T$ independent of $N$ such that every solution of the homogeneous recurrence $\sum_j\alpha_jY_{n+j}=0$ on the uniform grid $h=T/N$ satisfies

$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|Y_n\|_\infty\le M_T\max_{0\le j<k}\|Y_j\|_\infty.$$

Here $\|x\|_\infty=\max_{1\le i\le d}|x_i|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The root-condition equivalence for zero-stability is established separately.

For the method in [[def-linear-multistep-method-consistency-order-and-root-condition]], define

$$\mu_0=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_j,\qquad \mu_m=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jj^m-m\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_jj^{m-1}\quad(m\ge1).$$

For every integer $p\ge1$, the method has order at least $p$ if and only if $\mu_m=0$ for each $m=0,\ldots,p$. In particular, consistency is equivalent to $\rho(1)=0$ and $\rho'(1)=\sigma(1)$.

Let $C$ be the row-shift companion matrix for the monic polynomial $\rho/\alpha_k$, where $\rho$ is the characteristic polynomial of a $k$-step method. For a complex vector $v$, set $\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|$ and for a matrix $A$ set $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$. Then

$$\sup_{n\ge0}\|C^n\|_\infty<\infty$$

if and only if $\rho$ satisfies the root condition from [[def-linear-multistep-method-consistency-order-and-root-condition]]. Consequently the homogeneous recurrence is zero-stable exactly under that root condition.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$
